analysis.one_liner: Strips the President's power to cancel cross-border pipeline and power line permits without Congress's approval.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee; it was referred to three House committees and three subcommittees and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit any President from revoking a permit for an oil or gas pipeline, an electric transmission line, or any border-crossing part of those facilities, unless Congress itself passes a law authorizing the revocation. It covers permits issued under long-standing executive orders that govern projects crossing into Canada or Mexico. The practical effect is that a project like a cross-border oil pipeline, once permitted, could not be canceled by a future president acting alone. The bill was a response to a president using exactly that power to kill an international pipeline, and it was designed to prevent it from ever happening again.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that build and operate oil and gas pipelines and electric transmission lines crossing U.S. borders gain the most, because a permit they obtain could no longer be revoked by a later president without an act of Congress. That converts a revocable executive permission into something much closer to a permanent property right. Energy producers who ship oil and gas across borders also benefit, since their routes become harder to cancel.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the President from revoking a Presidential permit, or any permit required under executive orders, for constructing, connecting, operating, or maintaining an oil or natural gas pipeline, an electric transmission facility, or a border-crossing facility, unless an Act of Congress authorizes the revocation.

Covers permits under Executive Order 13337, 11423, 12038, 10485, and any other executive order governing cross-border energy facilities, so the protection reaches the full range of international energy projects.
Supporters framed the bill as protecting energy security, giving cross-border pipeline projects assurance that a change in administration cannot erase their permits.

analysis.who_pays: Communities and landowners along cross-border pipeline routes lose the strongest available off-ramp, since a president could no longer cancel a project over new safety, water, or treaty concerns without convincing both chambers of Congress to pass a law. The public also loses executive flexibility on climate and energy policy, and the rule would bind whichever party holds the White House.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities along pipeline routes and the public

drawbacks.text: It removes the President's ability to respond quickly if new information about a pipeline's safety, environmental harm, or treaty implications emerges; undoing a single permit decision would instead require passing a law through both chambers of Congress.

By making cross-border permits effectively irrevocable, the bill shifts the risk of long-lived energy infrastructure onto the public and future administrations rather than the companies that hold the permits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does address a real grievance — a president unilaterally erasing a permitted, partly built project strands billions in private investment and jobs. But its remedy is a one-way ratchet: pipeline developers get near-permanent permits, while the public's ability to cancel a project for newly discovered reasons depends on Congress agreeing to act. The benefit flows mainly to a concentrated industry; the cost is borne by whoever lives near the routes and by anyone who wants energy infrastructure decisions to remain reversible.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then three subcommittees, none of which took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg introduced the bill on December 8, 2021, joined on introduction by a dozen Republican colleagues, and it was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources Committees.
Within two weeks it was further referred to three subcommittees — Energy; Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials; and Energy and Mineral Resources.
No committee or subcommittee ever held a markup or advanced the bill, and no floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
All 14 cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's death leaves the status quo in place: any President retains the power to revoke cross-border energy permits without asking Congress, which is the outcome pipeline developers were trying to prevent. The industry gained nothing, but it also faced no new restriction; the clearest winners are whoever wants executive authority over pipelines preserved, and in practice that favored the administration and pipeline opponents of the era.

industries.industry: Cross-border oil and gas pipeline operators
industries.note: The bill would make a presidential permit for an international pipeline effectively irrevocable without Congress, converting a revocable permission into durable protection for pipeline investment. This follows a president revoking the Keystone XL permit, and the bill's gain for pipeline companies comes at the cost of communities' ability to see a project canceled when new concerns emerge.

industries.industry: Electric transmission utilities with international interconnections
industries.note: The bill covers border-crossing electric transmission facilities too, giving those owners the same permit protection. Because new cross-border transmission lines are often built to move low-cost power, locking in their permits can serve consumers, though it also shields any transmission project from future reconsideration.
